nodes.label: The caliphate
nodes.full: Medina, Damascus and Baghdad: it conquered the oases, expelled the Jews, ran the pilgrim roads, and — as its power faded — left the northwest to its tribes.
nodes.src: background — al-Balādhurī; the early Islamic administration of the Hejaz.

nodes.label: Egypt (Fatimid and Mamluk)
nodes.full: The power that held Egypt and, with it, the Egyptian Hajj road and much of the Syrian one: it garrisoned the stations, dug the wells and paid the route tribes.
nodes.src: background — Petersen, 'The Medieval and Ottoman Hajj Route' (2012).

nodes.label: The Hajj and the Ḥaramayn
nodes.full: The pilgrimage to Mecca: the reason the northwest mattered at all, the source of its economy and its sacred geography, and the traffic that wrote its rock inscriptions.
nodes.src: background — Peters, 'The Hajj' (1994).

nodes.label: The Muslim scholarly world
nodes.full: The geographers, the road-book compilers and the pilgrim travellers who described the corridor from outside — the region's only detailed medieval record.
nodes.src: background — Yāqūt; al-Muqaddasī; Ibn Jubayr.

nodes.label: The northwest under the caliphs
nodes.full: The conquered oases were held by governors from Medina and then Damascus; the Jews of Khaybar and Fadak were expelled under ʿUmar; and the region was demoted from a frontier to a pilgrim corridor between Syria and the holy cities.
nodes.src: al-Balādhurī, Futūḥ al-buldān; the early Islamic administration of the Hejaz.

nodes.label: Wādī al-Qurā and the early Islamic oases
nodes.full: 'The valley of the villages' and the string of oases along the route were a real agricultural district in the first Islamic centuries — taxed, settled and productive — before a long decline set in.
nodes.src: Yāqūt, Muʿjam al-buldān, on Wādī al-Qurā; al-Muqaddasī.

nodes.label: The bedouin northwest
nodes.full: As the caliphate weakened the region belonged to its tribes — the Balī, the Juhayna, the Banū ʿAṭiyya, and from the north the Shammar and the ʿAnaza — who held the wells and either taxed or raided the pilgrim caravans.
nodes.src: the tribal geographies in the medieval and later sources; Max von Oppenheim, 'Die Beduinen'.

nodes.label: Dūmat al-Jandal and the small emirates
nodes.full: The oasis of al-Jawf, held by the Kalb and then by others, was a minor emirate with its own fort — the Marid castle — at the far northern edge of the pilgrim world, where the routes to Syria and Iraq forked.
nodes.src: Yāqūt on Dūmat al-Jandal; the Italian–Saudi excavations of the Marid castle and the oasis.

nodes.label: The overlords of the Hajj roads
nodes.full: The caliphs, then the Fatimids and the sharifs, then above all the Mamluks of Egypt ran the Syrian and Egyptian pilgrim roads through the northwest — garrisoning the stations, digging the wells, and paying the tribes to let the caravans pass.
nodes.src: Suraiya Faroqhi and the earlier literature on the Hajj roads; Andrew Petersen, 'The Medieval and Ottoman Hajj Route'.

nodes.label: Qurḥ, Taymāʾ and Khaybar
nodes.full: Qurḥ (al-Mābiyāt) near old Dadān was a market town and a mint on the Hajj road through the 13th century; Taymāʾ held on under local families; and Khaybar, notoriously malarial, shrank to a fever-ridden group of villages.
nodes.src: the al-Mābiyāt / Qurḥ excavations; the medieval geographers on the oasis towns.

nodes.label: The expulsion of the Jews
nodes.full: ʿUmar removed the Jewish communities of Khaybar and Fadak to Syria and Iraq, on the tradition that the Prophet had said two religions could not remain in the Hejaz — the end of the ancient Jewish oases, and of the region's oldest continuous settlement.
nodes.src: al-Balādhurī; the debated historicity of the ʿUmar expulsion; Michael Lecker on the Khaybar Jews.

nodes.label: The tribes and the pilgrim caravans
nodes.full: The raiding of the Hajj caravans by the tribes of the route, the surra payments that bought passage, and the periodic massacres when a subsidy lapsed or a caravan lost its way — the chronic low war of the corridor for nine centuries.
nodes.src: the Hajj-disaster notices in the chronicles; Faroqhi, 'Pilgrims and Sultans' (1994) for the later pattern.

nodes.label: The wars of the bedouin northwest
nodes.full: The southward push of the Shammar and the ʿAnaza from the 15th century, and the feuds over the wells and the grazing that came with it, reshaped the tribal map of the region on the eve of the Ottoman period.
nodes.src: the tribal migration literature; the northern Arabian tribal geographies.

nodes.label: The Fadak affair
nodes.full: The oasis of Fadak, a personal estate of the Prophet, became a contested property — claimed by Fāṭima, held by the state, granted to the ʿAlids by sympathetic caliphs and taken back by others. A small oasis carried a large weight of Sunni–Shiʿi dispute.
nodes.src: al-Balādhurī and the Shiʿi sources on Fadak; the fullest treatment in Wilferd Madelung, 'The Succession to Muḥammad' (1997).

nodes.label: The administration of the Hajj roads
nodes.full: The amīr al-ḥajj of Damascus and of Cairo, the fixed stages, the wells and the small forts, and the surra to the tribes — the logistical machine that ran the pilgrimage reached down through the northwest and was most of what governed it.
nodes.src: Petersen, 'The Medieval and Ottoman Hajj Route in Jordan' (2012); the Hajj-road literature.

nodes.label: The surra and the tribal subsidy
nodes.full: The annual payment in money and grain from Damascus and Cairo to the tribes of the route was a transfer of wealth into a poor region in exchange for the caravans' safety — and the single largest economic fact of the medieval northwest.
nodes.src: the surra registers (later, Ottoman, with medieval roots); Faroqhi (1994).

nodes.label: Madāʾin Ṣāliḥ and the Thamūd
nodes.full: Medieval Muslims identified the Nabataean tombs of Hegra with the Qurʾanic people of Thamūd, destroyed for rejecting the prophet Ṣāliḥ. The site became a place of dread that pilgrims were told to hurry past without stopping or drinking its water.
nodes.src: the Qurʾan 7:73–79, 11:61–68; the ḥadīth of the Prophet hurrying his men past al-Ḥijr at Tabūk; Ibn Jubayr, Riḥla.

nodes.label: The pilgrim road as a religious landscape
nodes.full: The shrine of the prophet Ṣāliḥ, the mosque where the Prophet was said to have prayed at Tabūk, the local saints and the Sufi lodges of the route — a sacred geography laid over the corridor by the twice-yearly traffic of the Hajj.
nodes.src: the Hajj-guide literature (the dalīl al-Hajj); the shrine notices in the geographers.

nodes.label: The last Jews and the end of a presence
nodes.full: Small Jewish communities lingered at Taymāʾ and Wādī al-Qurā for some centuries after ʿUmar's expulsion, and a legend of a surviving Jewish tribe at Khaybar persisted into modern times — but the ancient Jewish northwest was effectively gone by the high medieval period.
nodes.src: the traveller reports chasing the Khaybar legend; Newby, 'A History of the Jews of Arabia' (1988).

nodes.label: The old town of al-ʿUlA
nodes.full: The dense labyrinth of mudbrick houses — sharing walls, roofed lanes, a single defensible mass — that grew up from the 13th century as Qurḥ declined. A classic Hejazi oasis town, inhabited until the 1980s and now conserved.
nodes.src: the al-ʿUlA old town conservation project (Royal Commission for AlUla); the earlier surveys by the Saudi antiquities department.

nodes.label: The early Islamic rock inscriptions
nodes.full: The enormous corpus of dated and undated Arabic graffiti along the routes — including some of the earliest dated Islamic inscriptions anywhere, such as the Zuhayr inscription of 24 AH (644–45) near al-ʿUlA, written a decade after the Prophet's death.
nodes.src: the Zuhayr inscription; the Saudi and international epigraphic surveys of the northwestern routes (Frédéric Imbert and others).

nodes.label: The Hajj-road wells and forts
nodes.full: The reservoirs, cisterns and small forts built and rebuilt along the two pilgrim roads by the caliphs, the Fatimids and the Mamluks — the medieval water and security infrastructure that the Ottomans inherited and expanded after 1517.
nodes.src: Petersen (2012); the archaeology of the pre-Ottoman Hajj stations.

nodes.label: Qurḥ, the vanished market town
nodes.full: The excavated remains of al-Mābiyāt — its houses, its congregational mosque, its pottery kilns and its coins — give the fullest picture of a medieval Hejazi town on the pilgrim road, abandoned by the 14th century and never rebuilt.
nodes.src: the al-Mābiyāt excavations (King Saud University; later the RCU); the Qurḥ coinage.

nodes.label: The geographers on the northwest
nodes.full: Al-Muqaddasī, al-Iṣṭakhrī, Yāqūt's Muʿjam al-buldān and the Hajj-road itineraries described the oases, the wells, the tribes and the distances of the corridor — a well-documented route through an otherwise thinly-documented land.
nodes.src: al-Muqaddasī, Aḥsan al-taqāsīm; Yāqūt, Muʿjam al-buldān; Ibn Rusta and the road-books.

nodes.label: The travellers on the road
nodes.full: Ibn Jubayr and Ibn Baṭṭūṭa passed through al-ʿUlA and Tabūk on the Hajj and left the classic descriptions of the corridor — Ibn Jubayr's account of the 'abode of Thamūd' at Madāʾin Ṣāliḥ among them.
nodes.src: Ibn Jubayr, Riḥla; Ibn Baṭṭūṭa, Riḥla.

nodes.label: The epigraphy of the route
nodes.full: The dated Kufic graffiti, read as historical documents, and the modern Saudi and international survey projects have made the northwestern routes one of the richest early-Islamic epigraphic landscapes anywhere in the world.
nodes.src: the OCIANA and Saudi epigraphic projects; Imbert on the graffiti of the Hejaz routes.

nodes.label: The Hajj-service economy
nodes.full: Provisioning the caravans, guiding and guarding them, keeping the wells, and selling dates and fodder to the pilgrims — the pilgrimage was the economy of the medieval northwest, and it arrived twice a year.
nodes.src: Faroqhi, 'Pilgrims and Sultans' (1994); F. E. Peters, 'The Hajj' (1994).

nodes.label: The shrinking oasis farmland
nodes.full: The date groves of the oases fed the towns and the caravans, but the irrigated area contracted over the medieval centuries as the population and the trade both fell — Wādī al-Qurā's 'villages' becoming fewer with each generation.
nodes.src: the settlement archaeology of the oases; the medieval geographers on the decline of Wādī al-Qurā.

nodes.label: The surra as the region's income
nodes.full: The annual subsidy from Damascus and Cairo to the tribes of the route was the largest single flow of money into the northwest — a corridor paid, year after year, to stay open.
nodes.src: the surra literature; Petersen (2012).

nodes.label: The wells and reservoirs of the route
nodes.full: The deep wells, the plastered reservoirs (birak) and the catchment channels along the two pilgrim roads — the water technology, built and rebuilt by successive overlords, that made the twice-yearly crossing of the waterless corridor possible.
nodes.src: Petersen (2012); the reservoir archaeology of the Syrian and Egyptian routes.

nodes.label: The oasis irrigation, maintained
nodes.full: The underground channels and well-and-bucket systems of the oasis towns, kept working through political collapse and economic decline by the oasis communities themselves — the quiet engineering that kept the corridor's few settled places settled.
nodes.src: the oasis hydrology surveys of al-ʿUlA and Khaybar.

nodes.label: The corridor between Syria, Egypt and the Ḥaramayn
nodes.full: The region's whole medieval significance was as the ground the two great Hajj roads crossed — the link, twice a year, between the Mamluk metropolis at Cairo, the caravan city of Damascus, and the holy cities of the Hejaz.
nodes.src: Peters, 'The Hajj' (1994); the route geography.

nodes.label: The pilgrim as a carrier of goods and news
nodes.full: The caravans that crossed the northwest carried trade goods, letters, books and gossip between Cairo, Damascus and Mecca, and the towns of the route were where that traffic paused, resupplied and exchanged news.
nodes.src: the studies of the Hajj as an information and trade network.

nodes.label: The tribes and the two capitals
nodes.full: The tribes of the route dealt directly with Damascus and Cairo over the surra, the escort contracts and the compensation for a raided caravan — a small-power diplomacy conducted from the desert with the greatest states of the age.
nodes.src: Faroqhi (1994); the Mamluk correspondence with the Hajj-road tribes.

nodes.label: A corridor, not a country
nodes.full: The medieval northwest had no state, no city of consequence and no history of its own beyond the two roads that crossed it — the clearest case in the peninsula of a region defined entirely by what passed through it.
nodes.src: the historiographical point is made across the Hajj-road literature; the region has no medieval chronicle of its own.

nodes.label: The deep continuity of the tribe
nodes.full: Through the caliphate, the Fatimids and the Mamluks, the human structure of the northwest — the tribes, the wells, the oasis families — barely changed. The overlords came and went; the corridor stayed the same.
nodes.src: the ethnographic and tribal-history literature on the northern Hejaz.

nodes.label: The thread continues — the Ottoman northwest and the railway
nodes.full: The folio ends in 1517, when the Ottomans took over the Hajj roads with Egypt. The Ottoman forts, the European travellers, the Hejaz Railway and the northwest's absorption into Saudi Arabia are covered in the Hejaz folios.
nodes.src: a forward reference: hejaz-1517-1900 (which carries the northwest oases and Hajj-road material forward) is already built.

nodes.label: The pilgrims on the road
nodes.full: The heat, the thirst, the bandits and the fever of Khaybar — the ordinary pilgrim's experience of the northwest was one of the hardest stretches of the journey to Mecca, and the chronicles and the graves along the route record how many did not make it.
nodes.src: the Hajj-disaster and pilgrim-mortality notices in the chronicles; Peters, 'The Hajj' (1994).

nodes.label: The tribes as guides and predators
nodes.full: The men of the Balī, the Juhayna and the Banū ʿUqba who guided, watered and guarded the caravans for a fee — and raided them when the fee was short — living on both sides of the same transaction, generation after generation.
nodes.src: Faroqhi (1994); the traveller accounts of the escort tribes.

nodes.label: The oasis women and the caravan slaves
nodes.full: The women of the shrinking oasis towns, working the date harvest and the household, and the enslaved people moving with the caravans and the trade toward Egypt and the Hejaz — the people the geographers and the pilgrim narratives pass over almost entirely.
nodes.src: the general household and slave-trade literature; the near-total silence of the sources on both.
